lines: Same table, two very different questions.
Watch how differently each one gets answered.
One order, found by its id, through an index that was already sitting there.
A handful of pages touched, and it is done before you would notice.
Now ask for a total instead, across every single row.
The index cannot help with that, so the engine has to walk the entire table.
That total only actually needs one column out of the six this table has.
So does the engine get to skip the other five, or does it read them anyway?
answer: It reads them anyway. A row's columns sit packed together in the same block on disk.
There is no way to grab just one column's bytes without pulling the whole row along with it.

lines: Here is exactly how little of each row that one column really is.
And none of that waste is a bug. It is just what storing by row means.
Flip the storage around, column by column instead of row by row, and the waste disappears.
Needing five columns out of a hundred now means reading roughly five percent of the table.
Splitting data into small tables is exactly what makes independent transactions cheap and safe.
That same split is also what forces a big aggregate query to stitch everything back together first.
Few rows, read whole, for point work. Few columns, read whole, for scans.
Carry that forward, because the next refresher names the relationships underneath both of them.
